utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Are you to take the next witness, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have him then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, before I begin with your examination, you and I speak the same language so I'd like to ask you to make pauses between question and answer and after that to begin your answer. This way we will enable the interpreters to do their job. Could you tell us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Branko Krga.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I was born on the 18th February, 1945, Daruvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: On 13 August 2007, did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Ojdanic and sign it in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you testify before this Court in the Milutinovic et al. case on the 3rd and 4th October, 2007?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of proofing for your testimony today, did you have occasion to read the transcript of your testimony in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: To all the questions asked of you in the Milutinovic case, would you answer in the same way if they were asked of you again today?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. May I ask that the statement of Mr. Krga, 006-0037, the testimony of Mr. Krga on the 3rd of August 2007 be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are tendering the statement of the 13th of August 2007?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's not the 3rd August. It's the 13th August 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be document Exhibit D00519. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the Trial Chamber to admit the transcript of the testimony of Mr. Krga in Milutinovic of the 3rd and 4th October 2007. We have two versions, one is the public version the other one is under seal. The public redacted version is D001-0178 -- 71. While the other one is D008-1970. The number of the redacted version is D011-1871.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: First the redacted version will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00520.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then the unredacted version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00521. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The unredacted version will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, correction, Exhibit D00521 is admitted under seal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will read a brief summary of Mr. Krga's evidence for today. In the course of his military service, the witness has occupied various command and staff positions in the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Yugoslavia. In the period from 2002 to 2005, he was Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. In the course of 1998, the witness was an advisor in the Ministry of Defence for Defence policies and international military co-operation. In mid-January 1999, he was appointed chief of the intelligence section of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Under full responsibility, the witness stated that he was not aware of the existence of any plan or any specific document or directive mentioning or referring in any way to expulsion or transfer of Kosovar Albanians from the Republic of Serbia or from the territory of Kosova-Metohija. During his tenure on the General Staff, he never attended any meeting that would have dealt with any such topic. The witness will further explain that in the year 1999 during the war when the problem with refugees came to a head, the General Staff of its own initiative issued a proclamation asking Kosovar Albanians not to leave their homes. He will cite operative data that the administration he was heading in 1999 gathered indicating the abuse of the refugee issue and the efforts made by the KLA to use the movement of refugees to cause a reaction of the international public and an aggression against the FRY. The witness states in his statements that the combat activities were exclusively targeting terrorists and the members of the KLA. When the aggression of the FRY started, the purpose of combat operations, in addition to fighting terrorists, was to defend the country from NATO air-strikes and to prepare for a defence against ground invasion. The witness will testify that the collegium of the staff of the Supreme Command regularly met once a week. From time to time, inter-meetings [as interpreted] of the staff were also organised. The witness submitted reports of these meetings almost every time, and the contents of his reports exclusively dealt with intelligence. In other words, the activities of foreign diplomatic and military representative, the writings and reporting of foreign media, and the way these activities reflected on the security and defence of the FRY. The witness will show on the basis of which intelligence the General Staff of the Army Yugoslavia made its war plans during the NATO aggression. The witness will testify on facts that were known to the Army of Yugoslavia concerning the way NATO forces assembled and prepared for a ground invasion on the border of the FRY with Macedonia and Albania. He will also speak about the role of Albania in providing equipment, training, and supplying arms to the KLA terrorists. The witness will testify about the information he had at his disposal about the co-operation and support provided by NATO countries, especially the US to the KLA, he will also give evidence on his contacts and activities with member countries of the NATO initiated by the Army of Yugoslavia in order to ensure a peaceful resolution of the crisis between February and March 1999. The witness will also testify about the constant insistence of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia that a peaceful solution be found to the aggression of NATO. The witness will testify that he was a member of the negotiating team on behalf of the Army of Yugoslavia in Kumanovo. This is a brief summary of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, were you a member of the Army of Yugoslavia; and if so, until when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Army of Serbia Montenegro until 18 February 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you retired on that date?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, pursuant to the law I had met all the requirements for a retirement pension and I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What rank did you hold at the moment of retirement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Colonel-general. In western terms it would be a four-star general.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What is your occupation today?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I'm a lecturer at a university school for diplomacy and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you briefly enumerate the positions you held in JNA and the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: During my service I occupied a variety of command and staff positions. I had two terms of office in diplomacy in Prague and in Moscow and in the last few years of my active service I occupied high positions in the General Staff in the defence ministry. I was chief of the intelligence administration and advisor to the minister concerning defence policy and international military co-operation. I was also Deputy Chief of the General Staff and Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, I'll repeat the question. Your answer is recorded properly. The question was could you briefly explain to which positions you were appointed within the JNA and the Army of Yugoslavia. Thank you for your answer. I would like to now deal with 1998 and 1999. Which exact positions did you have in the defence ministry in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: During 1998, I was advisor to the minister for defence policy and international military co-operation. And that duty meant that I dealt with matters of defence policy and co-operation on a military level with foreign countries. In addition to that, I had direct contacts with the minister and proposed various solutions to him linked to a change in the organisational structure of the ministry, the General Staff, and the army in general, and matters concerning our relations with other countries including the NATO alliance and many other organisations. The minister at that time was Pavle Bulatovic, and he accepted most of my proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, did you attend meetings of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: No. At that time, that is to say from 1993 up until 2003, the General Staff was not within the composition of the ministry. That is to say, the minister of defence was not superior to the Chief of the General Staff. The Chief of General Staff was directly linked to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So that I did not attend the collegiums of the Chief of the General Staff during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you now about the processes in the Ministry of Defence and the army. During 1998, was there a process to unify the Ministry of Defence and the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, especially after an agreement reached between Milosevic and Holbrooke. We understood that the time of peace had come and that we could undertake certain organisational changes of a substantive nature, and along those lines I proposed a project to unify the Ministry of Defence and the General Staff, to unite them. And this is something that required several months for everything to assume its proper place. However, for reasons that are generally known, the situation deteriorated and so we were not able to undertake that job at the time but we left it to several years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this action to unify or unite the Ministry of Defence with the General Staff, was that normal? Was it normal to do something like that in an army that was preparing for offensive activities or a possible war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: No, certainly not, because it would be impossible for the army to be engaged in some war conflicts in a stage whereby organisational processes were taking place and changes were taking place. You do things like that in stable periods when you expect a time of peace and when there was no need for any direct involvement on the part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, during 1998, the processes linked to the Special Forces corps, what happened there, do you have any information and knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, the corps of the Special Forces was one of the strongest forces at that level in the Army of Yugoslavia; and within its composition you had the special units, the Guards Brigade, the armoured brigade, and some other units. So it was a very powerful unit, a mighty unit. However, at the end of that same year, 1998, decision was made to disband it. And in the first few months of 1999, the unit was in fact disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you the question I asked you earlier on, a moment ago. The disbanding of the corps of the Special Forces, was that a customary move for an army that was preparing for any kind of offensive action or a war in the near future?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Certainly not. It was a measure that could be expected in peacetime under peaceful conditions in an environment that would enable this vast job to be dealt with smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's look at the Ministry of Defence. And in 1998 how did they view the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement in the ministry?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, the Ministry of Defence, the General Staff, the whole army, the whole country in actual fact, this was seen as lifting the burden. They were all very pleased and we, especially the professional soldiers, hoped that an armed conflict had been averted and that the problem would be resolved peacefully or, rather, through political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please you were in the Ministry of Defence, so you weren't in the General Staff, and you explained that position to us. Now, did you have any information whatsoever about the situation in Kosovo during 1998 in view of the fact that you were in the Ministry of Defence? And if you did, what information did you have and who did you obtain it from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Although the General Staff, as I said earlier on, was not subordinated to the Ministry of Defence, the minister of defence himself, as a member of the government, would of course receive information from the General Staff and the intelligence services and also from diplomatic representatives. So part of that information, I myself read. And I was therefore informed, if not fully, then to a great extent about the events that were going on at that time both in Kosovo and Metohija and generally speaking in that environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, as an advisor to the Ministry of Defence, did you attend any meetings which the minister had with foreign diplomats and foreign military representatives; and if so, at meetings of that kind, was anything discussed linked to Kosovo, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were a number of such meetings. And when the ambassador of a foreign country would come, he would be escorted by the military attaché and I would attend such meetings with the minister and they would discuss the security situation but also various forms of co-operation. And I remember one particular meeting after an incident and conflict that had broken out linked to the Jasharis. When the ambassador military attaché of Great Britain came to see the minister, this topic was discussed extensively. Everything -- everybody felt very uncomfortable that a situation like that had arisen in the first place, but it was noted that it was an anti-terrorist operation and they spoke about some of their experiences from similar operations in Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, forgive me for interrupting, Your Honours and my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Counsel is venturing into areas relating to the witness's exercise of his functions when he was in the Ministry of Defence and what he observed and what he did during that period of 1998. I don't recall seeing that in the summary and maybe I missed it, but actually I didn't bring my notes for that period because I didn't anticipate we were going to be dealing with his work in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the summary which I read out at the beginning before this witness's testimony began, it was clearly mentioned that he was during 1998 in the defence ministry and that he would be talking about his knowledge and experience working there. So I see no reason why we should not briefly deal with that particular period since the witness explained to us what the role of the Ministry of Defence was compared to the General Staff and the army in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you point to any particular passage in the summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. It's paragraph 2. In the course of 1998: "The witness was an advisor in the Ministry of Defence for defence policy and international co-operation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That tells us his position. The issue is whether it indicated you were to discuss his activities in that role.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We only stated the function he performed. His post. And so I'm asking him now whether he attended any meetings and whether he has any knowledge about things like that, and the witness is recalling one such meeting but I'm not going to dwell on it and I'm going to move on to 1999. But I was just interested to hear whether he was informed about the situation in Kosovo at that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we understand you are now moving on to 1999, Mr. Popovic? That avoids the difficulty then, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so, Your Honour. We are moving on to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you explain to us in greater detail the situation in the Army of Yugoslavia, what that was like, and the situation in Kosova-Metohija at a point in time when you were appointed chief of the intelligence administration in the General Staff which is January 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I've already said, at the end of 1998 and the beginning of 1999, in the ministry, the General Staff, and the army, there was a certain mood of optimism with respect to the resolution of the crisis in Kosova-Metohija, and this was based on the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement. And we sincerely hoped that the situation would be resolved, as had been agreed through peaceful means, that is. However, already in mid-January of that year, 1999 and later on, various incidents began to take place and this gave us cause for concern with respect to further developments. We knew, of course, that in October 1998 an armed conflict was narrowly avoided, and we were afraid that a situation would crop up whereby that would be the outcome again.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you now to explain to us the role of the intelligence administration within the frameworks of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: The intelligence administration or the intelligence component within the structure of the General Staff, as in any other country, has the prime task of monitoring the security situation in an area. And to weigh it up, to assess the dangers and the threat to the country's security. And that's the kind of work we did too. In addition to that, as the chief of the intelligence administration, I myself, was, if I can put it this way, the host to foreign military attachés and I had almost daily contact with them. They came to see me, we discussed the situation, we discussed the problems, and I can say that most of them shared our conviction that the situation was becoming more complicated. And we sought ways and means of avoiding any possible conflicts. Now, the knowledge that I gained and information I gained, I would inform the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff, and if there were any more important questions, I would inform the members of the Supreme Defence Council, the defence minister, and some other state officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the way in which the administration functioned, the intelligence administration, we will deal with that in greater detail when we come to analyse the documents that I'm going to put to you. But I'd like now briefly to ask you to tell us how you went about gathering information, the information that you sent on further to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Information came from various sources. Public announcements by various international forum, the governments of foreign countries, various statements made by high-ranking state officials, media and so on and so forth; but we mostly relied on our own intelligence sources via intelligence offices abroad and in the country, and we also used electronic reconnaissance and monitoring for the gathering of information as well as reconnaissance of the troops on the ground. Also we had a number of contacts and co-operation with foreign intelligence services. We exchanged visits and information so that that was another way in which we gained important information and intelligence. All this intelligence was -- well, we used the customary technology, we would analyse and process the information coming in, we would weigh it up to assess how far the information was realistic and truthful or not, and if we thought they were realistic, then we would set the information out in our reports and analyses and so on and so forth and send them on to the people I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This intelligence that you gathered, did it serve you and the General Staff in the making of plans or strategies, whatever, and if so, could you give us a few details?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Any serious plan concerning the security made in the General Staff would first analyse the situation and the threats that it posed. It would be followed by a presentation of the possible engagement of the army to neutralise such threats. Mine was a very responsible role, namely to present to the General Staff the situation in the territory concerned, and to suggest measures that could be taken to avoid surprise attack and preserve our security.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any specific plans that you mean when you say that, or are you describing the way you considered such intelligence generally and used it in making plans?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Our General Staff, like many other staffs, had a number of plans. And all these plans concerning the security of the country featured in the first position an analysis and suggestions. Of course, there were plans concerning staffing and replenishment that did not need intelligence to be included in the first paragraph. But whenever an engagement of units was involved, then intelligence was a necessary component.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say in your answer "like many other General Staffs perhaps our General Staff had a great number of plans," could you explain further what you mean by that? And also tell us if there were a number of such plans, on what would the use of any such plan depend?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: It all depended on the various threats to the country. There were plans to defend from aerial attack, plans of defence in case of a ground invasion, plans of defence against attacks from various directions and sources. Most of these plans, since I worked in the General Staff for a long time, never were implemented because the threat envisaged never materialised. But it's simply a rule and a custom that armies make contingency plans for all sorts of situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now move to a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask the Usher for his assistance. The Defence, Your Honours, has again prepared a binder with the documents we will be using. And with your leave, we would like to hand the binder to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, any time I call a document, I will give you the tab number for you so you will be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up in e-court P1337.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: For you, General, it's tab 2. We can see on the screen the collegium, session of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army held on 14 January 1999. Can you explain briefly what is the collegium of the Chief of General Staff and how often did this collegium meet in January 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Collegium of the Chief of the General Staff is one of the methods of work wherein usually once a week all chiefs of various administrations and sectors would be -- were meeting to analyse the situation in the country and in the army, and this meeting would make certain conclusions, after which the Chief of the General Staff would issue instructions as to how to realise these conclusions. As I said, this collegium met normally once a week and sometimes more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6, please, in the B/C/S, and page 6 in English. This is page 5 in B/C/S, we need 6. We have the right page in English now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Here you speak, General, and you say: "In the reactions of western countries regarding the activities of Siptar extremists and the kidnapping of Yugoslav Army soldiers, the western countries mostly demanded the cessation of all military activities and the start of a dialogue but did not explicitly condemn the so-called KLA, which was particularly obvious when the US blocked the statement from the UN Security Council chair on the activities of this organisation." Could you tell us briefly what this was about and on what information you based this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I said, we followed very carefully statements issued by various institutions in international relations, primarily the UN, the OSCE, the European Union, NATO, and we conveyed these positions to our authorities. I would inform the General Staff. Although, of course, members of the General Staff could find out about it from the media. But it was my responsibility in case any of them missed it, to brief members of the collegium of the positions of foreign authorities. In this case it concerned the reactions to kidnappings of our soldiers. Namely, on the 8th of January, Albanian terrorists kidnapped a number of our soldiers and we considered that as a violation of our agreement and something that could only deteriorate instead of defuse tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the last paragraph on page 6, which is page 7, paragraph 4, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, here you say: "The engagement of Albania in the solving of the Kosovo and Metohija issue (mediation between the representatives of the political parties from Kosovo and Metohija in order to come to a unified political platform) confirms the continued instrumentalisation of this country by the US which is in this manner trying to strengthen the Siptar negotiating position. In addition to providing increasingly open support to the secessionists, the Albanian leadership is trying to use these activities to stabilise the political situation in the country ..." Can you explain this further, you said that you always began your briefs by an analysis? Can we just wait a little.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I was saying, we followed very carefully Albanian reactions to the developments in Kosovo and Metohija, I believe it was quite natural bearing in mind the links between Albania and the ethnic Albanians in this province. Every action had a special dimension because it could contribute to either escalating or improving the situation. We followed the reactions in Albania itself because many of these reactions were conditioned by internal affairs of that country which were very complex at the time and burdened with many problems. It was our estimate that by emphasising the problem of Kosovo and Metohija, various factors in Albania were trying, through expressions of patriotism and other feelings for their compatriots in Kosovo and Metohija, were trying to position themselves as an adequate representative of the Albanian people within their own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll continue with page 7, paragraph 2. In English it's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "The bringing in and deployment of the announced contingent of the verifiers extraction forces as part of the Joint Guarantor Operation has been finalised. According to our information, about 1.850 people over 40 armoured personnel carriers and 23 helicopters have arrived in Macedonia so far." What is this about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: We know that the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement envisaged the Verification Mission of about 2.000 people to be sent to Kosovo and Metohija. The mandate of that mission included the so-called Joint Guarantor Operation, that is, bringing in forces that would have a protective role and provide assistance during evacuations and such. We, of course, monitored these activities to check whether they were implemented as agreed or perhaps there were some other forces being brought to Macedonia that had nothing to do with this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to move now to page 8 in B/C/S and page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Here we see a conclusion, items 1, 2, and 3. Item 1 says that finding a political solution to the crisis is still complicated because major powers do not display any readiness at this moment to exert any strong pressures on the Siptars, especially the KLA, to stop with the terrorist actions. And before you give us your comment, please look also at item 3 which says that the political support offered under the influence of the US by the Albanian officials to the so-called KLA is on the increase. In this connection, training and equipping of Siptar extremists in the north of the country is continuing and the aim is to transfer them to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: First of all, I want to say that we were united in our conclusion that only the political solution is the right solution. And it was in this light that we viewed all the on-going activities. We feared an escalation of these conflicts, which, in the end, unfortunately happened with all the consequences. We were certain at that moment - and I think I would make the same conclusion now - that the international community could have exerted more pressure on the Albanian extremists, and if it had done so, the situation would have been diffused. We were very sensitive to any support given to their activities, especially training them and providing equipment to these groups for insertion to Kosovo and Metohija, because we knew that this could lead to new incidents that we certainly hoped would happen -- wouldn't happen because they, as we knew, would further complicate the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have Exhibit P902 pulled up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's document number 3 in your set. General, there we have the collegium, the 9th Session of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, held on the 21st of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the second page in the B/C/S -- no, page 6 in the B/C/S. I apologise. Page 6, please, which is page 7, the penultimate paragraph, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, if we look at paragraph 2, Lieutenant-General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic is saying something. Who was Colonel-General Dimitrijevic, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: At the time, he was the chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in paragraph 2 he says, the action in the village of Racak on the 15th of January in the presidential announcement to the Security Council states that the operation was carried out by the SFRY security forces, in other words the Yugoslav army and the organs of MUP of the Republic of Serbia. Now, in the following paragraph, when Milan Obradovic -- it's Milorad Obradovic. Yes, I beg your pardon. Milorad Obradovic says -- goes on to say, General, officially at the federal commission, there was discussion about that, and as far as I know, nobody mentioned the army nor was the army involved in anything, at least to the best of my knowledge. Now, General, sir, were they in fact discussing what had happened in Racak on the 15th of January as Aleksandar Dimitrijevic say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: The substance of the discussion here is twofold. The first thing discussed was what had actually happened in Racak because, as we all know, this caused great unrest in the world. And secondly, they analysed to see whether the army played any role. The goal, of course, was to establish the actual facts so that steps could be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we look at page 8 in the Serbian version, which is page 10 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And we are going to see what Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic says. General, Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic, what was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic at that point in time was the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He says: "After this action or operation or whatever you want to call it linked to the village of Racak, I was intrigued about this and I asked the corps commander personally to send me a report on where the army was and what the army was doing at that moment. It had to be studied in detail, and I studied this report, and then I went back to the special report which was received from information on the 15th and 16th of January, and from the 1st, the 2nd and the 3rd, the most important one, it says that the army did not take part." Now, the Chief of the General Staff here, is he talking about the information he received about the events in Racak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, as is common knowledge in the army, there is a system of reporting and sending information from bottom to the top. So any possible engagement of the army in any event, the subordinate must inform his superior thereof. And the Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic, as we can see from this, received those reports from the subordinate commands. And from that it would follow that the army did not take part in that action around Racak. Of course, General Ojdanic certainly insisted upon establishing -- well, he was fully conscious of all the adverse repercussions that could follow, so he insisted on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's digress for a moment, but we'll come back to the events in Racak. Now, in the following paragraph, General Ojdanic says as follows: "The essence is that there is no reason for the army commander or this General Staff to hide anything, things that are done must be known. If we participated, we'll say that we did, and if we need suffer the consequences for that, we will suffer them, but we must know why this is being done ..." Now, General, was this the position taken by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia linked to everything that happens in the army and everything that the General Staff is in charge of and deals with?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the General Staff was fully conscious of the fact that nothing can be hidden and that anything that happens will out sooner or later. And so we see that the Chief of the General Staff here found it necessary to highlight that legal and professional and moral relationship of the superior and subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's move on to page 9 of the B/C/S, which is page 11 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's the part where you had something to say. And in the first paragraph you say: "A military envoy here claims that he personally saw the artillery shooting in the sector around Racak village." That's number one. And then in paragraph 3, you say: "I also agree that we must absolute know exactly what went on, these are very serious issues, so we must know absolutely correctly what the information is on what happened."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, immediately after the event in Racak, there were different interpretations as to what happened there, how many victims there were, who the victims were, who took part in the actions, so on and so forth. And from my contacts with foreign military representatives, and this was one of them, this military envoy, I came to the conclusion that the situation was indeed serious and that we had to clear it up so that we could tell the military envoys and the public at large and all the state institutions and anybody else what the truth about those events was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now move on to page 11 of the B/C/S, which is page 13 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you, once again, take the floor at this meeting and say the following: "General, the main characteristic in the reactions of the international factors to the latest escalation in Kosovo and Metohija and concerning Racak village is that all the relevant fora, including the Security Council, have come out with a statement, which is somewhat unusual for a conflict at this level." And then in the following paragraph you say: "This is the result of the influence of American diplomacy and the media." And then in paragraph 3: "The speed and manner of reaction to the events in the village of Racak reveal extensive co-ordination in the matter, which must be borne in mind in the further development of the situation and possible similar new cases." General, may we have your comments to these statements made by you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, we were really very concerned by the reactions to the -- well, we were concerned about the event itself, and then reactions to the event. And we analysed who reacted, what their reactions were, how speedy the reactions were, what the contents of the messages were; and from that we deduced that there were elements of co-ordination which worried us quite a lot because we knew from earlier incidents and from previous statements made by Albanian extremists that they would like to see various conflicts and clashes to happen which would be a pretext for NATO's involvement, of course on their side, against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now staying with those same pages, in paragraph 4, on the last sentence there, you say: "The United States of America are endeavouring to assert NATO's credibility on its 50th anniversary which will be celebrated in April of this year. Now translated into practical terms, this means that NATO will endeavour to achieve something in Kosovo and Metohija which would serve to confirm its existence." Could you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: From the reactions of high ranking American representatives and from the reactions in the media and on the basis of contacts with a large number of diplomatic representatives, frequent mention was made of NATO's credibility, that NATO's credibility was important and that NATO's credibility should be saved. Now, I understood the NATO member states' endeavours along those lines, but in response to this position of theirs, I would reply and say that the best way of preserving NATO's credibility would be to see that the problems in Kosovo and Metohija even under NATO pressure were resolved peacefully through political means. I considered that to be best for both NATO and Yugoslavia and for the Albanians living in Kosovo and Metohija as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, you say: "In the command of the 5th ATAF command in Vicenza and the command of the South European front in Naples, alert -- the level of alert has been raised and reconnaissance activities of the NATO air forces increased as part of Operation Eagle Eye." Could you tell us what operation this was, Operation Eagle Eye?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: On the basis of the agreement we mentioned, of October 1998, it envisaged the possibility of having the NATO air forces over-fly the air-space on the territory of Yugoslavia, FRY, and that was Operation Eagle Eye. And let me just mention that on the basis of that agreement, it was envisaged that NATO representatives should be present in the command of the air force and anti-air defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and they really were in the command and followed and monitored the events as they were happening. Now, we saw what NATO's reactions were and followed them closely because through their activities we tried to see what the next steps would be and how that could reflect on our own country's security.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: NATO force movements that are mentioned here, and we are dealing with the 21st of January, 1999, here, those movements, did they -- were they cause for concern, and did they indicate and did they give you a premonition of what was to come?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I've said, we followed all movements closely, all NATO movements closely, and on the basis of those movements, the movement of air forces, naval forces, and ground forces, we tried to assess what actions could follow. We knew that NATO was a very mighty, powerful organisation and that even in peacetime deployment -- with it's peacetime deployment it could go into action. It had the power to act. So any movements were cause for additional concern. So we analysed their movements to see what would happen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page in the B/C/S and the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you go on to say: "On the territory of Albania, measures of raised alert can be noted, forces -- reserve forces have been brought in, there is additional mobilisation, and rapid training of reserve forces is being carried out in the territory of north-east Albania." May we have your comments there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, as I've already stated, we followed what was going on in Albania with particular tension. Their armed forces which were fairly weak, albeit, as we can see, nevertheless, were engaged in some sort of activity. And very often we would conclude that they were intentionally going about these actions to exert additional pressure on our country. Because, you know, if activities were being carried out, if combat readiness was being raised, if mobilisation was underway and training underway, rapid additional training for the reserve forces, then anybody monitoring those activities would be concerned as to the object of those measures, what they wanted to achieve by carrying all that out. So when we mention rapid training in north-east Albania which is Peshkopia, that general area, those settlements, we monitored the situation and we drew certain conclusions, how this could be reflected in Kosovo, because Kosovo is in close proximity to the location where this rapid training was being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph you say: "A new element in Albania is the engagement of" -- this is the 21st of January. "The new element in Albania is the engagement of Italian armed forces in the formation of refugee centres and camps." What did such conduct of the Italian armed forces indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I had a rather good and intensive co-operation with Italians. Around that time, I went for a visit to Italy, I spoke to my counter-parts in the military and intelligence services, and I thought they were rather concerned about the developments in Kosovo and Metohija. They had already realised that one of the consequences of an extended conflict could be a flow of refugees. At that time, the number of refugees was not so great, but they estimated that if the conflict escalated, the number of refugees could increase. Another key reason why Italy in particular was sensitive to this problem is that a large number of Albanian refugees, even in the past, moved through Italy. They would take the ship to Italy, disembark in Italy, and created certain problems for the authorities there. And in case the conflict escalated, the problem could really increase. So they wanted to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph are conclusions. In the second conclusion, we read this: "Some new cases might be rigged, for instance, a humanitarian or some other such disaster which could again cause the escalation of the situation." What did you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: The developments in the former Yugoslavia during the war were full of various orchestrated incidents involving large numbers of deaths, and we were afraid that in addition to what happened in Racak, something else could happen to cause uproar in the international community and provoke NATO to react, and we constantly warned our units on the ground to be alert and to avoid being dragged into a conflict that could get out of hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now call D006-0051.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your number 4, General. This is a session of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia held on the 28 January 1999. Could you please turn to page 4, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, that would be page 5, paragraph 5 in B/C/S and the one but last paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You said this: "However, it has been noticed over the past few days that some foreign factors are beginning to accuse also the KLA for orchestrating or rigging the incident in Racak." Tell us, General, what information did you subsequently get about Racak? Where does this come from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I can say that many players in the international community were making efforts to gain an objective view of the situation, and some of them reacted in this way. Some prominent individuals and leaders and politicians in foreign countries had great misgivings about the possibility of a worsening conflict, and they voiced opinions that the KLA was deliberately escalating its activities and incidents, and provoking the Yugoslav Army. For each of these references, I had a source. I cannot tell you now which international representative said what exactly, but there were a number of them. Many of them accused us, but we tried to take into account also those who had a more objective view and made certain accusations against the KLA as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: On the same page, it's paragraph 6 in B/C/S, you say that a total number of planes was increased from 264 to 392. Were you concerned by this increase in the number of aircraft? What did that tell you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I said, we were very serious and attentive in monitoring the activities of the NATO forces around our country, and they did have quite a respectable forces, even without reinforcement, on airfields around Yugoslavia. And whenever we saw an escalation, we were concerned because we thought that was an indicator of additional pressure, on the one hand, but also possible preparation for an armed operation. And of course it was a great concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not be finished with this document before the break, therefore, we might as well take it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take the break now. It's the normal time. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we are continuing with the collegium meeting of the 28th of January, 1999. Let us look at page 5 in the B/C/S, page 6 in English. Paragraph 2 in B/C/S and paragraph 3 in English. This is what you say: "In the period to follow, we are to expect -- we are to expect --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel give us a reference in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 5, paragraph 2 and paragraph 3 on page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read this out again. "In the period to follow, we are to expect the harmonisation of pressures and the acceptance of solutions with the threat of using military force combined with permanent escalation of political and economic sanctions. In this way, the operationalisation of the strategy of military threat continues."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This is a conclusion as to what can be expected in the period to follow. We expected these pressures to continue, and the operationalisation of the military threat implied a number of measures destined to demonstrate this military threat. That's what we discussed before, bringing in more forces, various media announcements and statements, which was enough to make the threat real, rather than just verbal.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at paragraph 4 on the same page in B/C/S. It's also paragraph 4 in English. In the last sentence you say: "However, if some massacre or some undesirable incident were to occur again, were to be rigged again, it would make it worse." Can you give us your comment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, we were deeply aware that any action, any event similar to that in Racak or some other incidents we had seen in battle-fields earlier would be a new pretext for a media campaign against Yugoslavia, but could also cause some concrete steps to be taken against our country. Of course, that would happen if Yugoslavia were to be accused of causing such an incident. So we sent many warnings and instructions to units to beware of such provocations because that could only hurt our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for page 11 in B/C/S and page 13 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Again, it's a passage where you speak, General. And in paragraph 1 you say: "First, in view of the course, the crises being resolved, there are dozens of variants and possibilities in play and there are all sorts of things. There is something that is called reality, there is trickery, and I would like to draw your attention to these, we simply should not believe everything that the media comes up with." Could you explain this, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This shows, again, how responsible we were in our attitude to everything that was happening around us, everything reported in the media and elsewhere. We registered, as I say here, that there are many options in how the situation might develop, and I wanted to warn my colleagues from the collegium that they should not believe everything they hear and read in the media, but that they should try instead to gain an objective view of developments, because the media were reporting in a wide variety of ways and it was certainly undesirable to rely on the media reports alone, especially for us in the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document shall be given Exhibit D00522. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have the next document, which is P1333, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's document number 5 in your set, and it is the interim session of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army held on the 2nd of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we turn to page 4 in the B/C/S, please, which is page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And I'd like us to look at paragraph 5 or the penultimate paragraph in the English where you say the following: "In the interests of the defence of the country, we therefore believe that the third option is the most realistic, to propose to the state leadership that we should participate in the negotiations but that we should clearly define our conditions, especially with regard to protecting our sovereignty, putting an end to the NATO threats, and avoiding the arrival of these forces in the territory of Kosovo ..." Now, General, could you clarify the position presented in this paragraph, which options were available, and was that the position generally taken by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: It was a period prior to the Rambouillet negotiations, and from our point of view, we analysed how the situation might develop. It was a political question first an foremost, and it was up to the state organs to deal with it, but we thought that it would be useful to analyse what kind of turn the situation could take. And as I say there, there were different options open and we discussed and evaluated these options and decided that the best option was to go to the negotiations and to try and find a solution to the situation that way. Now, as far as the reference to NATO forces coming into Kosovo, at the time, there was the fear that if these forces were brought in, they would give the Albanians the possibility of achieving their pretensions, the pretensions they had in the area, and what we see happening now, the cessation of that part of the territory from the FRY. Let me remind you that during the time of the negotiations, the president of the day of Serbia, President Milutinovic, mentioned that NATO forces might be brought in to Yugoslav territory once Yugoslav becomes a member of NATO, but as we know, the agreement was never reached. And so our fears were linked to that, and we relied on a statement made by the state -- secretary of state of the USA Madeleine Albright to the effect that the Albanians themselves were boasting and bragging and they said that the main goal of bringing in NATO forces to Kosovo and Metohija, that that was the main aim and that their requirements would then be met, the requirements made in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us about the things the Albanians boasted about, on the basis of intelligence gathered, did you have information to the effect that the Albanians were discussing these positions with other factors?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, we did have information to that effect, and it was on the basis of that intelligence that I said what I did here.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's look at document D006, a Defence document, 0118. D006-0118.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we have before us a document titled "Assessment of the Intelligence and Security Situation and the Danger to the Security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." First tell me if you are familiar with this document and whether your intelligence administration took part in compiling it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This is a document that was drafted from time to time when the situation was deemed to be complex and that it needed more detailed analysis than was possible at the collegium meetings. And then pursuant to an order from the Chief of the General Staff, various institutions would be given a task of each preparing its contribution for this document, this assessment. And all the information was harmonised and dovetailed and we see that this was done at the level of the sector for operations of staff affairs, the first administration, and this is one of those assessments. And the intelligence administration, which I headed, took part in that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page D006-0122 in B/C/S, please, and D006-0161 in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, in your set of documents this -- it is the assessment of the intelligence assessment situation under point 1, the influence of the foreign factor or of the -- the influence of the foreign factor and the subparagraph is titled "Influence of the International Community At Large and Its Organisations." Now, my question to you is, was this subject part of what your intelligence administration dealt with in assessing and appraising the intelligence and security situation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that did come under the remit of the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have D006-0140 in the B/C/S version displayed, please, and D006-0181 for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's towards the end of the document where we have the section titled conclusions. That's right. And could you focus on paragraphs 3, 4, and 5. "Foreign armed forces in the region, and particularly those that are occasionally deployed in the area, may exert great pressure and have considerable influence on the political processes, and, under certain circumstances, might be used in various forms of military intervention against our country. "The disposition and activities of the foreign armed forces in the region indicate that the southern part of the FRY faces the greatest threat." And then: "From the point of view of national Defence, our primary objective should be to avoid the deployment of foreign armed forces in our territory and in particular an armed conflict with NATO, and at the same time to preserve our vital government and national interests." May we have your comments to what I've just read out, especially with respect to an avoidance of a conflict with NATO?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: The conclusions set out here is the logical result of what I was saying earlier on; the situation was already very complex at that time, and it was our view that the armed forces could have this kind of effect on our country. Now, we soldiers were attached to the idea of having the problem solved through a peaceful solution, through political means, and we availed ourselves of every opportunity to avoid an armed conflict with NATO. We, of course, knew full well the strength that NATO had, NATO's might. And when we compared that to the forces we had, we came to the conclusion that a conflict with NATO would be highly detrimental to our country, and we knew that the former battlefronts of the former Yugoslavia, we knew what the outcome there was, so we were absolutely in favour of a peaceful solution to solving the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is not an exhibit already?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00523. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we next have Exhibit P1341, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's document number 7 in your set. This is a collegium meeting of the Chiefs of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia held on the 25th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 3 in the B/C/S displayed please, which is page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you to take a look at paragraph 4 there, on page 3 that is, which is the penultimate paragraph in the English. It says: "Various pieces of information indicate that, these foreign troops would not completely disarm the so-called KLA. The Albanians are even bragging that Ms. Albright had promised them that NATO troops will make sure that they hold a referendum, even if there were no such provision in the agreement." General, a moment ago you were telling us about this position and the information you received. Just briefly, does this reflect the actual situation linked to bringing in NATO troops to the territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, we could say that it does reflect the conclusions that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 4 in the B/C/S, which is page 5 in the English. And I'd like us to look at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, in the last paragraph you say the following: "Finally, General, I would suggest that the collegium consider the possibility of proposing to our state leadership that representatives of the General Staff be included in the preparation of our delegation for the next stage of the negotiations during which highly important military issues will most probably be addressed, primarily the issue of the status of the Army of Yugoslavia and the role of the military in general in the implementation of a future agreement. In that respect, there is no one else more qualified or more responsible than us." May we have your comments to that, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Following on from the USA delegation and others, and their example, we saw that the diplomats were accompanied by military experts. So I had a number of meetings -- or we had a number of meetings with General Clark, General Anderson, and others who would come to our country together with Mr. Holbrooke, for example. And we concluded that it would be a good idea if our delegation included military men for the reasons stipulated here. However, that did not happen, and I think that was a mistake. It wasn't a good thing that the soldiers weren't represented there because they would have contributed their military knowledge and professional knowledge and realistic attitude and would help resolve the situation in a better way than it was, in fact, dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have Defence Exhibit D008-3977.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is document number 8 in your set, General. Now, General, we see that this is a report on the intentions of the so-called KLA which was sent to the General Staff on the 9th of March, 1999. Before we undertake a more detailed analysis of this report, could you first please explain to us report or piece of information, what does that mean and what did this particular one contain?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: The report or information was one of the publications published by the intelligence administration. There were various bulletins, rules of service, and so on. But when we have something which was called "informatia" or information report, there were two types. The first type was a daily report, and the second type of information sent out was one that dealt with just one subject. And the one we are looking at is the latter, so it dealt with just one subject and that was here the intentions of the KLA. And you see who it was addressed to and sent to, the addressees were those persons whom we considered to be interested in this kind of information. So it wasn't sent out to everybody, as we would do in case of the daily regular reports. So this was a piece of information obtained through intelligence sources saying that the Albanians or the KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to that. We'll look at it in greater detail. In paragraph 1 it says: "The incidents along the border and the conflicts between the Army of Yugoslavia MUP of Serbia carried out by the so-called KLA and ambushes and so on, is carried out by the KLA for -- to recruit new members, attain media support, and to intensify the collection of financial assistance from the Siptars in the diaspora." Could you just tell us more about the general security situations and the facts stated in the first part of this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, everything that was indicated here actually happened. Kidnappings, killings, media propaganda, recruitment of new members, et cetera. It was clear over a longer stretch that the Albanians were hoping for and expecting a NATO intervention because only with that could they attain their goals, that is, the creation of a separate territory and cessation from Yugoslavia, as well as independence. They must have reckoned that if peace were to be negotiated and if we had returned to the negotiating table, these objectives of theirs would not be so easy to attain, and we see statements from that time made by the representatives of Albanians that confirmed this. So that there is a continuity in their thinking, namely that their objectives were attainable only with foreign assistance and NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 2 of this report we read the following: "With foreign assistance, the so-called KLA has drafted plans for staging a massacre of innocent Siptars and members of the OSCE, which would, they believe, provide a legitimate basis for activating the forces to extract the verifiers, and thus the entry of a NATO ground force into Kosovo and Metohija. In addition, the leadership of the so-called KLA, in line with NATO preferences, are also taking steps to paint a picture of humanitarian catastrophe in this connection, many villages have been abandoned under pressure, beside the villages Gorance, Rezance, Pustenik, Krivenik, Ivaja, Ljac, Kotlina, and Straza. The plans also envisaged the inhabitants to move out of the villages of the Lepenac river valley, Kovacevac, Dicevac, Dubrava, and Vata, and Slatina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This information we also obtained from sources on the ground, and it clearly shows that by staging this humanitarian catastrophe which they believed could give a pretext for a NATO intervention, they also exerted pressure on their own fellow citizens and made them move out of many villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd also like to look at the last paragraphs of this report. It says: "There is indicia that the so-called KLA, estimating that these villages are already empty and it makes sense to exert pressure to evacuate them, is planning attacks on major settlements which would create the effect of an exodus and would provoke reactions by the Army of Yugoslavia and the Ministry of the Interior, giving NATO a reason to intervene. The preparation of camps for refugees in the north of Albania and in Macedonia indicates that this information on the preparation of a new humanitarian catastrophe is correct."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the scenario we've been discussing for a while. They were looking for a good reason for the NATO to intervene, and one good reason would be humanitarian catastrophe, the death or evacuation of a large number of ethnic Albanians, and that's why they were doing what they were doing. Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I tender this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00524. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now call up D157.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's your tab 9. This is a document from the Kosovo Verification Mission, the date is 26 February through 4 March 1999. On page 1 we see the subheading "KLA." It says: "It seems that over 100 members of the KLA crossed the border in combined with the said militia while encouraging the locals to leave. The incentive to move into this region is unclear, although a number of possibilities exist. By encouraging the movement of internally displaced persons, the international media was able to claim a Serb offensive was underway." On the next page in B/C/S it says: "Indeed, Euro News reported that a Serb offensive had started and accompanied this with images of Serbian vehicles on the move and locals on the road with sad faces. It was a good move for the welfare of ethnic Albanians. The Albanian daily "Koha Ditore" described Kacanik village as a ghost town, which the verifiers recorded as an untruth. And the first reports from the region implied in a certain way that there had been a massacre." Now, General, can you tell us something about this and about the media manipulation involved here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This shows very eloquently that the KVM was perfectly aware of these manipulation attempts by Albanians, and I would particularly like to emphasise this last sentence, namely "the first reports implied in some way that there had been a massacre." This seems to indicate that their attempt at manipulation was at first successful. However, it was later established that this was not true, and the media reported on that as well. We also had our own information from the ground, and we were able to confirm or to deny all this media speculation. A very renowned medium such as the Euro News accepted, in this case, the Albanian interpretation. Regrettably, they were not alone, there were many such cases where the media, without going into the essence of things and without checking their information, reported immediately, accepting somebody's version, and confused the public about what was really going on in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Such information, did it also affect your views in the intelligence administration about the general picture in -- created by the foreign media?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I've already told you that we monitored official statements, but we also followed media reporting, foreign media and our media. But in many such cases when the stories were obviously untrue, we realised that we should not use the media as our main source of information. We should just monitor them as an expression of their views and their attitude. This was evident in the case of Racak and many other cases later. We were perfectly aware that the situations on the ground was nothing like the reports. And unfortunately the media compromised themselves, broadcasting inaccurate information. And that affected our view of the media. We became so suspicious that even when the media reported something perfectly accurately, we did not take their word for it because there had been so many cases of manipulation before.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P965.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's your tab 10. This is a session of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia held on 11 March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to page 5 in B/C/S and page 7 in English. In English it's paragraph 2, and paragraph 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Here you say the following: "Among the forces around us, new developments have taken place. A Joint Command was formed in Skopje on the 4th of March, and they were placed under the command of General Jackson. In keeping with their plans, he should also be the commander if new Kosovo forces are formed. New units are brought in in these rapid reaction forces and there are already 9.500 personnel in Macedonia."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to the forces we identified as support forces for the Verification Mission, other forces began to arrive in Macedonia, namely the command that was established, headed by General Jackson, and the number of personnel in Macedonia at the time caused us concern as to the really intentions of these forces, why they were accumulating in that area, why there was no official notification to us. And, of course, we continued to watch them intensively, and unfortunately all we were able to see was that the forces were being built up.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 6 in B/C/S. And page 7 in English stays. We'll be discussing the last but one paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You say this: "I suggest, General, to consider the possibility of holding a briefing for foreign representatives, perhaps next week when the situation is clearer, primarily regarding our positions on the main issues, namely the bringing in of forces into Kosovo and Metohija. And we again propose to consider the possibility that a representative of the Army of Yugoslavia be included into our delegation for the next round of negotiations because we believe military issues are now coming up on the agenda, and it would be a good idea for us to be represented." General, what kind of briefings are you referring to here, and if they were indeed held, what were the effects?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: It is a regular custom in diplomacy that the host country holds briefings for ambassadors, military attachés and other diplomatic personnel. These briefings are held to familiarise them with some new development such as an event or a new law passed, perhaps, or something else. And we also held these briefings from time to time when we thought necessary or perhaps at their request. I was usually the one who hold these briefings. We would invite all military attachés. I would brief them on the situation and give them a chance to ask questions that I would take or one of my colleague, and in that respect we had a rather good co-operation with military attachés. They would inform in turn their defence ministries and their General Staffs. And what they learned at these briefings was an element that they could use in making their own estimates of the situation and the crisis. There was one interesting situation when, after a briefing, the American and British military attachés came to see me a few days later and said that all that I had told them was indeed correct because in the meantime they had visited Kosovo and Metohija and verified my information. Of course, we always made every effort to provide accurate information, as a matter of principle, but also because we knew that they could easily check all that we said and there was no point in telling them anything that wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
