utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now go to the next document, P1339. May we have it pulled up on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's number 11 in your set. It's a collegium, session of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army held on the 18th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we have page 3 of the B/C/S, which is page 4, paragraph 6, of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you say the following: "Most of the foreign diplomatic representatives and analysts believe that the initial situation regarding the continuation of negotiations on Kosmet implies an extremely uncertain outcome. The foreign factor will attempt to direct the developments in the field in tune with the course of the talks, especially if there should be a serious impasse due to the process." And this would serve the purpose of justifying their threat of using armed force against our country so that it could be forced to accept an imposed solution." I'm going to read out one more paragraph which I believe is closely linked to what you said, to cut this short: "As far as the forces in the area are concerned, the introduction of new rapid-reaction units from the NATO corps into Macedonia has continued and so far around 1200 men have arrived." Now, it says what they wish to achieve with this number, or, rather, what did they wish to achieve by having this number of men placed at the borders of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This was the 18th of March, we can see, which was a week before the NATO forces attacked the FRY. And the NATO forces that were brought into Macedonia were later found to be KFOR forces which entered Kosovo after the agreement. Now, General Jackson over there told us in Kumanovo that they had been in Macedonia for three months already and that they were waiting to enter our territory. Of course, at the time, we were not able to be 100 per cent certain that those were the forces in question, that is to say on the basis of the agreement that was supposed to enter Kosovo and Metohija, because through the media and other intelligence channels, the idea would be launched from time to time about the possibility of a ground force operation against our country, so we were very concerned and monitored the deployment of these 12.000 men into Macedonia right next to our border.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's move on to page 4, paragraph 2, of the B/C/S, which is page 5, paragraph 4, of the English. Paragraph 4 from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, here it says that as far as military pressures goes, it will continue and at some point in the negotiations they might even go a step further than Rambouillet and threaten to use force in such a way as to have all the factors of aggression against the FRY put into action. And this would lead to the withdrawal of the verifiers to Macedonia, the transfer of authority for air-strikes from Solana to Clark, and a 48-hour combat readiness would be introduced and even reduced, et cetera. May we have your comments to that paragraph about information linked to these options and finally whether that proved to be true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, everything that I stated here on the 18th of March from the 24th of March onwards proved to be correct later.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: One more paragraph, staying on that page, the last paragraph on page 5 of the English. It says: "This could come about if a Serbian delegation were to be accused of being the sole culprit for the failure of the negotiations, and if new clashes were to be provoked in Kosovo with a larger number of victims, destruction, and refugees, and possible attacks on the verifiers and border skirmishes and incidents." Did this prove to be true? Did this come about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately this was later confirmed to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have page 6 of the B/C/S version, please, which is page 8 of the English, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, here we can see Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic speaking, and he is referring to certain events. And in paragraph 3 he says as follows: "After that, Clark said that he wanted to convey to me a very serious problem which is that the Yugoslav Army will be destroyed if it enters into a conflict with NATO. If that were to be requested from NATO, all the depots, barracks, and forces of the Yugoslav Army will be destroyed." Now, my first question to you is this: Do you know that General Ojdanic had communication with General Clark, and if so, how was this communication effected?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that, and they had communication in two ways. The first was by way of an exchange of letters, they exchanged letters, correspondence, and then there were telephone conversations between the two. I was present during two such telephone conversations between General Ojdanic and General Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in keeping with that, I'm going to ask you to comment a few more documents which are closely related to what Mr. Ojdanic referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that, may we have Defence Exhibit D006-0215, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And in your set, it is document number 12, General. Looking at this document, we can see that it is dated the 22nd of March, 1999, and it says: "Enclosed with this document we are sending you an Official Note about the telephone conversation held between the Chief of the General Staff Yugoslav Army, Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic, and the commander of the NATO forces for Europe, General Wesley Clark."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's look at D006-0233 in the B/C/S version which is D006-0238 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it says the Chief of the General Staff General Ojdanic in his conversation said as follows. "However, since in our area NATO forces are being accumulated and we are openly being threatened with the use of force, it is our duty to do everything in our power to defends ourselves." We are talking about the 22nd of March, two days prior to the start of the NATO campaign. Can you just comment on this position taken by General Ojdanic briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was a very difficult time. However, I have to say at this point that at that time in Belgrade, Mr. Holbrooke was visiting, together with General Anderson and some other representatives, and negotiations were taking place there with the political leadership of Yugoslavia led by President Milosevic. I have to say that there was a glimmer of hope despite everything that was going on in the area linked to the armed forces and so on that at the 11th hour a political solution would indeed be found. Unfortunately, that did not happen. General Clark, during those negotiations, openly threatened General Ojdanic as is stated here, he said that in a few days time, he would completely route the Army of Yugoslavia if NATO forces became involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, as we don't have the page up on our screens that we are dealing with --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 3 or D006-0217 in the B/C/S version, which is page D006-0220 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down when quoting numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a fairly tense atmosphere. I remember that General Ojdanic called General Clark to come to Belgrade to discuss the accusations held by General Clark, accusations of the army. He did not speak of any humanitarian catastrophe at the time. He mostly referred to alleged lack of respect for the agreement reached in October 1998 in the sense of units leaving the barracks or a larger number of units in the field, et cetera. So at the proposal of General Ojdanic, we considered that this should not be a valid reason for the start of a war, and that is why he invited General Clark to come to Belgrade so that he could see on the spot what the situation was like and that they could discuss all this, however, General Clark's reply was that he couldn't go to Belgrade because that could be interpreted as pressure of a kind. I think this response from him was not a logical one, had no meaning or sense because at that time in Belgrade, there were visits by General -- by Mr. Holbrooke and many others with him, so the arrival of Clark in Belgrade wouldn't be seen as any additional pressure, but as an attempt to find a solution to a major problem that was looming. I can also add that in a previous conversation, General Clark invited General Ojdanic to travel to Brussels to discuss these various issues. Now, we suggested to General Ojdanic that he should take General Clark up on his invitation to go to Brussels, and I think to this day that that would have been a wise move. However, it never came about. I can't say for what reasons exactly, because I'm not fully informed of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00525. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have Exhibit D006-0239 up on our screens now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is number 13 in your set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we've got the wrong number recorded which means that the wrong document has appeared on the screens. The document I need is D006-0221. I might have misspoken and given you the wrong number, so I apologise if that is the case. Yes, that's right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we have before us a document also dated the 22nd of March 1999, and it reads: "Please forward in the usual manner the enclosed letter of the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic, to the NATO supreme allied commander for Europe, Colonel-General Wesley Clark." Now, looking at this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to the last page, which is D006-0223 in the B/C/S, and in the English the page number is D006-0238. That's it, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read -- but let me ask you first, are you familiar with the fact that General Ojdanic sent a letter of this kind to the commander of the NATO forces, General Wesley Clark?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, it was a letter sent after the negotiations held on the previous day that we discussed a moment ago. And we put it to General Ojdanic that he should make another last-minute attempt to transcend the situation and to send a letter to Wesley Clark. And that is what this letter is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General Ojdanic writes the following in one of the paragraphs: "The possible bombing of -- the Siptar terrorists would see the possible bombing as a signal to attack the remaining Serbian population of Kosovo and Metohija, the Yugoslav Army and MUP who would then respond fiercely, which would lead to new unnecessary casualties, conflicts, and other problems with unforeseen consequences." Was that the position taken by the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, and is General Ojdanic warning of the consequences that might ensue if there were to be an attack and bombing by NATO?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, anybody who gave it some thought, and particularly it was clear to the soldiers, that if NATO were to attack, that this would create an atmosphere -- a very difficult atmosphere and climate and that it would allow those who wanted to to expand the conflict with new provocations and to make the army and police need to respond, which would very serious consequences. And this is actually what happened during that unfortunate war. There's no doubt here that General Ojdanic wanted to ask General Clark to wield his influence once more and to prevail upon him to find a political solution rather than move on to a conflict, because without a doubt, a conflict is always the worst option. An armed conflict is always the worst option, and Clausewitz's definition, the well known definition that war is the continuation of politics with other means, in this case we could say that war had compromised politics because we know what it all led to ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely bearing in mind with what you've just told us, the next sentence in the following paragraph reads as follows: "The problem is a complex one, but it's solution is possible only through political means." Does that underline once again the way in which the problem should be solved?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That was a permanent view in the General Staff, that political solutions should be sought because that would be the only real solution to the problem. Any other scenario would be highly problematic and would -- and the situation that ensued confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I ask this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00526. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see D006-0239.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's your tab 14. We can see that the document is called "Brief 2/99," and before we move to a more detailed analysis of this document, could you please explain what kind of document is this to be called briefing number 2/99?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Of course. This is not really a document. This is a draft, an aide-memoire that I used for my briefing as the chief of the Supreme Command because it was called Supreme Command from the moment when the war began. And it was created based on the information we received during the day. The intelligence administration that I headed, continuously worked to fill in the facts which enabled me to always provide the most up-to-date information. This document was not submitted to anyone. It was not filed anywhere or recorded anywhere, and it shouldn't even be called a document. I must say, I'm a bit surprised that this paper found its way here, not being a document. Some things here I crossed out, some I added. The situation was so tense that I needed something like an aide-memoire to give my presentation to the collegium. In peacetime, I would jot down my notes in my own notebook; but during the war, my colleagues prepared this draft for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that one thing be clarified. I'm not sure if I heard correctly what is here represented at page 57, line 3. Or line 2. It said "I used for my briefing as the chief of the Supreme Command" as if he is describing himself as the chief of some body called the Supreme Command. It might be important, so I wonder if it could be clarified because I'm not sure that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. We'll clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You were talking about the purpose of these briefings. What purpose did they serve to you and what was your position at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: With the beginning of the war, as I said already, in fact, I said before that in peacetime we had collegium meetings once a week and during the war we had at least one a day, always in the evening. It was not a classical collegium meeting, although it was mostly the same people from the General Staff that analysed the situation. As usual, at collegium meetings, I would be the first to give a briefing to acquaint the members of the collegium with the situation in the region, with the developments, the forces of the NATO, plans for the future, et cetera, and then we would analyse the situation in the army, which steps needed to be taken and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just answer what was your exact position at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: In peacetime, I was chief of the intelligence administration directly responsible to the Chief of the General Staff. In war-time establishment, I was chief of the intelligence section of that war-time General Staff, and I was under the chief of sector for operations and staff affairs. So I was not directly linked to the Chief of the General Staff as in peacetime. It was an idiosyncrasy at the time. Later it was changed, the war-time establishment was changed. But at the time, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this clarifies the transcript. Could you please look at paragraph 6 of this paper which says: "If this does not happen, according to some reports, very rigorous sanctions would be introduced against the FRY, while others say the third phase of the operation would be activated - NATO ground forces entering Kosovo and Metohija by force." This -- the date of this document is March 1999. We can see that on one of the later pages. Were there any indications, however, that there would be a further NATO ground attack against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, we had our own channels of information, but also the media reported that the ground invasion was possible. I already said that we closely monitored the bringing in of NATO forces into Macedonia, and when we compared all the various information, it all seemed to indicate that a ground invasion was possible. Later on, as the war progressed, they gave up on that idea, but there were times when there was a heightened expectation of a ground invasion which made us wary, but also made us take additional measures, such as increased mobilisation and build-up of the army, not only in the area of Kosovo and Metohija but in the territory of the entire Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00527. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call D006-0272.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your tab 15, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can see that it's a couple of minutes to the usual break time, perhaps we should not start with the analysis of this document before the break. I have quite a few questions on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will look at our break now, but, Mr. Popovic, how are you going for time?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going very well, Your Honour. I will do my best to speed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you were going very well, you would be finished by now. Two hours was indicated for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right. However, and I suppose this e-mail reached the Trial Chamber as well, the Defence has already given up on some witnesses that were to testify on some of the same subjects as this one, and we are going to try to use as few witnesses to gain as much information as we can, and that is why the examination of some of these witnesses might take a bit longer. And we believe this witness is a case in point for which I apologise in advance. But we will certainly not exceed the time allocated to our Defence case. In fact, I'm pretty sure that it will be shortened in total. And that is why we are trying to get as much information out of a fewer number of witnesses avoiding us calling more of them. I hope it will overall speed up the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Popovic. It would be helpful to the Chamber if in the next few days there could be some more accurate indication of what witnesses were not to be pursued and your time estimates because we are having to make future plannings depending on timing, and if there is to be some significant change in the witnesses you are to call, we need to take that into account. We will adjourn now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we'll go back to the document called briefing number 6/99 of 28 March 1999. At the end of paragraph 1 it says: "All types of aircraft were used in the attacks, including B-52s, that is, including seven B-52s; 12 F-117s; and, for the first time, four EC-130s; and an undetermined number of A-10 Thunderbolts." Can you tell us about this last plane?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: That is a special type of aircraft intended to broadcast propaganda messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What are Thunderbolts, A-10 Thunderbolts, does it have any special purpose?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: These aircraft, thunderbolts, are in support of ground troops, in combat, mainly against armoured personnel carriers and tanks. They also used ammunition including depleted uranium.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information that such ammunition was used in the territory of Kosovo, and if so, what kind of information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This type of ammunition was also used in Kosovo and Metohija, but it was used outside of Kosovo in the rest of Yugoslavia. In Kosovo, there are many locations where such ammunition was used but primarily the area between Pec, Djakovica, and Prizren. Outside of Kosovo and Metohija, there were five locations in the area of the town of Vranje. We inspected these locations, and, as Chief of General Staff, I personally went there to evaluate the ground on those five locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you speak of your role as Chief of General Staff, what time-period would that be?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: That would be from mid-2002 until the beginning of 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at paragraph 4, it says: "For that purpose, Clinton held a meeting today with the members of the National Security Council, and a meeting of NATO experts is scheduled to take place tomorrow in London, where it is emphasised, recommendations will be made for entering Kosovo and Metohija by force, If they assess that our forces in Kosovo and Metohija have increased to 50.000, and the number of refugees to 500.000, over which there is much speculation." First of all, can you tell us something about these speculations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: What you call speculation was pervasive before and during the war. First of all, there were attempts to prove that indeed in that area a humanitarian catastrophe was taking place and that it was the forces of the FRY, the police and the army that are responsible. This number of 500.000 was something like a target. If the number of half a million refugees was reached, that would have been enough for ground forces to invade Kosovo and Metohija. Later on, things happened to be differently. It didn't happen that way. But in the first days of the war, this is the speculation that circulated widely in the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Since we are on the subject of speculation, can you tell me whether you know that there existed an Operation Horseshoe, called Operation Horseshoe? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. That was within the context of those speculations that were being made to put it to the public that the forces of Yugoslavia had an operation prepared in advance called Operation Horseshoe. The term used was actually a Croatian term rather than a Serbian term, and what they wanted to show was that an operation involving armed forces was being organised geared towards the ethnic cleansing of Albanians. Of course, no such operation was ever planned or executed. And later on, through the media and in other ways, they gave up on mentioning that particular operation. We concluded that on the basis of Clark's caution and warning that he would route the Yugoslav Army in the space of three days, when that didn't happen as he had announced, then they suddenly started to favour the term humanitarian catastrophe. They kept bandying about the term humanitarian catastrophe and the enormous number of refugees as so on. They put that out and wanted to justify the further involvement of NATO forces in that way and to create the opinion among the international public, principally the countries that took part in the attack, to justify a continuation of those operations by claiming that there was a humanitarian catastrophe afoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have Defence Exhibit 006-0383 put up, please. I think there was an error in the transcript. The number is D006-0383. That's right, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, just briefly on this document, it is dated the 30th of March, 1999, and it is a warning with respect to the taking of steps, and it says: "NATO planners," in paragraph 2, "are counting on good results because the Siptars have about 200 laser target markers. They will maintain communication with NATO officers through satellite telephones that were left behind by the verifiers when they retreated from Kosovo and Metohija." May we have your comments linked to the links between NATO officers, verifiers, and the rest?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As we can see, this is a piece of information from the commander of the corps from Pristina, and they arrived at this intelligence, and we received information to that same effect from other sources, that is to say that those links had been established and that they were functioning during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00529.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have D006-0276 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's document number 17 in your set, General. This is briefing number 10/99 of the 30th of March, 1999, and what I'm interested in is the penultimate paragraph which says that NATO, on the 29th of March, in formal terms, changed its intentions for the forces in Macedonia, some 15.000 soldiers, so that officially they are no longer intended there for peacekeeping purposes, but for combat tasks. May we have your comments?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, yes, that falls within what I was saying earlier on, that is to say that Clark's intention to resolve the situation in two or three days' time, to have the forces enter Kosovo probably as peace forces first on the basis of an agreement, and since that did not succeed, then they took on the character of combat units in actual fact, and their equipment, armaments, composition, everything, indicated that that's what they were, according to our intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at the last paragraph on that same page in the B/C/S, I think it's on the following page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "In parallel with continuing the air operations and preparations for carrying out a land operation, there is increasingly visible readiness among the leading western countries to stop the aggression, for which the most favourable option is being sought. Furthermore, a growing number of countries has offered to mediate in finding a solution for starting the negotiations." Now, linked to that paragraph, the one I've just read out, and bearing in mind what you have told us thus far in your testimony, as far as the contacts that you had with different diplomats and military attachés, can these initiatives at mediation be understood in that way and be brought in connection with the paragraph I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly they can. Just before the beginning of the war, I had contacts with American, German, and Italian and other representatives, diplomats, and others, with the idea of wielding as much influence as they could to prevent a war from breaking out. They had -- they showed understanding for this kind of initiative, but the reactions mostly were that it was a little late in the day and that matters had already come to a head and were out of control and that the peace option wasn't a viable one at that point. So this was yet another attempt of that kind whereby the military attaché of Italy came to see me and conveyed a message from the Italian side, and probably from NATO as well as an institution, that the general mood was that a peaceful solution should nonetheless be sought. Of course, what he told me I conveyed to the relevant authority, but unfortunately, the situation developed unfavourably and a solution was not found. We also had contacts through some British and other mediators who also wished to intervene to find a peaceful solution. The United States of America, too, sent various envoys to try and help find a solution. There were German, Italian, and other ones, but unfortunately, it did not bear fruit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender that document into evidence too, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00530, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have Defence Exhibit 007-4143 next, please. 007-4143 is the number, once again. Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's the right document, General. It's number 18 in your set. It is information number 22 dated the 31st of March, 1999. And just briefly, my question to you relates to item 3: "The B-1B bombers, whose arrival in the region was announced, will use cluster bombs with IC fuses against the armoured mechanised units," infrared fuses. Did that come to pass? Was it proved correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, not only attacking armoured mechanised units, but many other targets, cluster bombs were used against them, and unfortunately not all the remnants or cluster bombs have been cleared up from the area to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point in time, I'd like to use a document during the examination-in-chief of this witness which was not on the 65 ter list provided by the Defence. We did provide the Prosecutor with the document yesterday, and it is in e-court, but we conducted a search and came up with this document and we believe it to be useful in the examination of this witness. It is 65 ter 1974. And it is a report from the BBC News of the 1st of April, 1999. If you consider that we can utilise this document in this way and if there's no objection from the Prosecution, then I'd like to continue along those lines and examine the witness about this document, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is document number 21 in your set. It's a newspaper article published on the BBC News website after a press conference attended and held by the minister of defence of Great Britain. The foreign minister, Mr. Robin Cook and General John Drewienkiewicz, as it says in this article, the former chief of the OSCE mission in Kosovo. Now, tell me, please, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, since the document is in English and we don't have a translation in Serbian, speaks about expulsions and looting of Albanians taking place in Kosovo during that time, and the period is the end of March. Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I go ahead with my question, Your Honour, the Defence document number is D011-2268. It's got a new number. 2168. D -- That's right. That's the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: As a source of information for you intelligence service, press conferences of this type or newspaper articles and the like that were published on the Internet or in the papers, what value did you attach to them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: It would be normal that press conferences given by the foreign minister or defence minister or general of a major country should be noted with due attention and that the press conference should quote correct and precise data. However, we saw that there was gross exaggeration at those press conferences, and we remember one such occasion when there were rumours straightaway about 100 thousand people dead and I don't know how many hundred thousand refugees and persons raped and so on which was not at all the case in reality. So that these press conferences instead of being taken seriously were usually taken with -- as being just one more piece of information which we had to verify and check out ourselves. And very often we found that incorrect data and untruths were being presented. So, unfortunately, that's what the situation was like. It was not a good situation, and one would have expected, if somebody makes a statement from a high level, that they would be presenting true and correct data, not information that exaggerated certain events with -- as a form of executing their own hidden agenda, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony so far and in the documents that we've looked at and tendered into evidence, we see a number of ways in which the media could be manipulated. Could you tell us briefly what the reasons were for which you took information of this kind with a pinch of salt, that you considered them to be unreliable and that you needed to check them out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned during my testimony here today the problem over Racak and the attempts made to paint an impression about a humanitarian catastrophe at a time when that was not the case. There were not that many refugees at that period, so it was obvious that the object of these statements was to justify what was being done on the ground in the eyes of the international public. I can't claim now that it was done intentionally with the aim of intentionally deluding public opinion and the international public, but without a doubt that is in fact what happened. Public opinion was abused in that way about the actual facts on the ground. And this was enormously detrimental to having the crisis resolved, because it flared -- the conflict flared up that way, it fanned the flames of the conflict, and even if there was some truth or when there was some truth in the announcements made, they weren't taken seriously on our part, and I think there could have been other ways in which the representatives of foreign countries could resolve the situation or help us resolve the situation in context with us and impart information to us through their official services, information which should lead and could lead to a change of conduct on our part; that was omitted and the whole thing was reduced to a sort of media information and it triggered reaction on our part the way it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00532.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up D006-0279.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's your number 22, General. Briefing number 14/99 dated 1st April, 1999. In paragraph 1 it says: "The attack on the bridge in Novi Sad expanded the list of targets to include business facilities and elements of infrastructure by extending the strikes to include civilian infrastructure, the aggressor has gun with retribution and it will be increasingly difficult for them to justify their further actions before the international public." Could you comment briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, that fits in with what I said before. Within two or three days they did not manage to crush our forces completely as had been their plan and therefore they extended the list of targets. And they began to conduct air-strikes against civilian targets far from Kosovo and Metohija, in Belgrade, in Novi Sad, and in other towns. Since there was no military logic to it, we understood it as a sort of retaliation, retribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00533.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, I would like D006-0270.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is your number 23. This is report number 37 dated 3 April 1999. It says: "There are indicia that the NATO is planning to terrorise the civilian population by air-strikes and thus cause a major exodus over the next seven to ten days to the centre of Serbia, Albania, and Macedonia. It is assessed that after that the army of Yugoslavia units and a small part of the population would be more or less all that remained in Kosovo and Metohija, which would enable them to mount decisive air-strikes with the use of chemical agents, in order to completely destroy the VJ units located in the area." Can you comment on this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This is one of the reports we got from the ground that they obtained information that seemed to support this scenario. As we know now, it did not actually happen, but this was certainly one of the options that was considered, to separate the civilians from our units, thus making our units an easier target. They would then be more open to attacks from all sorts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph we read that: "Using confidential sources, western intelligence services are planting information among the Siptars, the ethnic Albanians, in the diaspora to the effect that the NATO would begin within 24 to 48 hours with indiscriminate bombing to raze Kosovo to the ground."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the propaganda messages probably aimed at intimidating our units or causing whatever reaction they had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00534.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-0281 would be our next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's your number 24, briefing number 19/99, dated 3rd April, 1999. We'll turn to page 2 immediately, both in B/C/S and in English, conclusions and proposals. It says: "In view of the possible damage the aggressor could inflict on us and the fact that they are conducting all sorts of experiments and venting their frustration, I consider it is in our primary interest for a diplomatic initiative to be launched as and as soon as possible. "1. In order to avoid being demonised in the media, I propose that our border authorities organise points for the reception of Siptar refugees who are returning to Kosovo and Metohija." Could you tell us more about this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I've already told you that it was -- it had always been our position that a diplomatic initiative is the only way to go. And as for this proposal to set up admission points for refugees, we had previously recorded their departure from the FRY and their return. They were moving around in circles. So we came to the conclusion that it would be a good idea for the army and the MUP and our authorities to organise admission points and to organise their return, wherever they wanted to go, and to provide appropriate media coverage so that the world can see that not only are we not expelling, but we are taking back these people who are trying to return home. This was not a setup or a media trick. It was a sincere attempt to deal with the problem that had become evident by that time, an attempt to receive back those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to tender this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00535.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may I ask for D008 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D008-3650.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is briefing number 21/99. Let's look at paragraph 2: "There are manipulations concerning the deployment of a large NATO force to Albania in Albania up to 6.000, which would be engaged in a peacekeeping mission to create the conditions for the return of Siptar refugees within the framework of a so-called humanitarian operation. This should be seen as linked to the existence of plans for the conduct of a step-by-step operation. Siptar terrorists entering from Albania and Macedonia are to take control of the part of Kosovo and Metohija and create the conditions for the introduction of ground forces. Some sources indicate that the Siptars have been set in motion as part of this plan in order to separate them from the VJ units which have become open targets for the aggressor." Now, there is mention here of the 4th of April. What information did you have of the 4th of April to confirm this information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: We often mention that there was no ground invasion during that time, but in a sense, a land operation did take place, and it was carried out by Albanian extremists from Albania on the axis of Kosara and it lasted for over a month. But since it was unsuccessful, another attempt was made on the axis of Morina. It was a major operation with involvement of Albanian extremists from Albania. We understood it was their objective to send this man into a ground attack, push back our forces from that region, and then NATO forces would be invited to take their place in the region as some sort of peacekeepers or peacemakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to the next page in B/C/S and in English. In English it's para 5, proposals, and then item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: "Refute that there is a humanitarian disaster, an allegation used in the west to justify the aggression and prepare a ground operation." Did you indeed have information to confirm these allegations, and what was the purpose of citing a humanitarian catastrophe?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: There were many reports pushing the idea of a humanitarian catastrophe and calling for air-strikes. The ground invasion was still an option at the time. It was our estimate that this whole insistence on a humanitarian catastrophe was driven by this objective, and that's why I proposed that it is our job to present a real picture to the public at home and abroad. But it was not a humanitarian catastrophe caused by anything we did, but it was as a result of the war that engulfed the entire country, including the capital Belgrade and the fact that our families too were occasionally refugees in the sense that they had to leave their homes from time to time as many other citizens. We were all targets and all of us could be said to be affected by humanitarian problems and tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the next page in B/C/S and in English. A draft communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please, focus on the first paragraph where it says: "The Army of Yugoslavia is not carrying out any sort of ethnic cleansing but is only responding to terrorist provocations. As the terrorists have broken up -- have been broken up, the Yugoslav Army has halted these activities and is now focusing on preparations for defence against the aggression and against the deployment of ground forces with which we are being threatened daily. When these threats cease, the VJ units will return to their peacetime garrisons and downsize to the usual level." Was this indeed the position of the Army of Yugoslavia and their explanation for the current situation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This reflected our general sentiment that armed activities should cease as soon as possible, that the troops should return to garrison, and the level of troops should be reduced to peacetime levels. We were not very happy that additional mobilisation had been carried out and all the other things that increased threats imply. In this way, we wanted to send a message and explain how we wish the situation to develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Another sentence in paragraph 2 is important, the last sentence which says: "We too have a position on refugees, and it's simply this, return to your homes." Was this a clear statement of your position, a position held widely by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly we really wanted these refugees to go home because we knew that staying long in the open air or in refugee columns is being blamed on us and the best solution for us was for them to return home and that this should cease to be a pretext for continued air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00536, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, we've gone five minutes over. It seems now that we must adjourn for the day. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
